abstract: Geographic body size variation, classically framed as Bergmann's rule, is a fundamental indicator of temperature-mediated morphological adaptation. However, empirical support for Bergmann's rule in birds remains highly unpredictable across lineages. We hypothesized that this variation is caused by differences in thermal similarity among species within the same genus, which may limit temperature driven changes in body size and be influenced by ecological factors. Using a global dataset comprising 5,715 bird species across 513 genera, we observed that thermal similarity was the strongest predictor of variation in the strength of Bergmann's rule among competing hypotheses. Among genera exhibiting significantly negative body mass temperature relationships, higher thermal similarity was consistently associated with less negative slopes, indicating weaker Bergmannian clines. Subgroup analyses indicated that the positive thermal similarity slope association was supported in dense and semi open habitats and among nonmigratory birds, but was not clearly supported in open habitats or among migratory birds. Our findings provide a novel explanation for variation in the strength of Bergmannian clines among avian lineages, showing that stronger morphological differentiation along thermal gradients is associated with greater thermal contrast. Consequently, our findings provide a basis for testing whether incorporating thermal similarity and ecological context can improve forecasts of avian morphological responses to ongoing climate change.
